ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Additional funds to South Central Railway for passenger 
amenities 
*241. SHRI NANDIYELLIAH: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether South Central Railway approached Railway Board for grant of 
additional funds to the tune of Rs. 20 crores during the current year for various 
passenger amenities; 
(b) if so, whether Government would assure of releasing this additional grant for 
the current year; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI R. 
VELU): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement

Railway for passenger amenities works during 2004-05. Accordingly, the funds allotted 
to South Central Railway under plan head Passenger Amenities was increased 
from Rs. 13.66 crore in the Budget Grant to Rs. 27.90 crore in the Revised 
Grant.

NACO to remove bottlenecks 
*242. SHRIMATI S.G INDIRA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the National AIDS Control Organisation 
(NACO) had offered a unique option to remove bottlenecks, streamline 
communications and ensure better utilization of funds; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the NACO had signed any Memorandum of Understanding with 
UNICEF in this regard; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
The National AIDS Control Programme Phase-ll gives the highest priority to 
generating awareness on HIV/AIDS issues through communication and social 
mobilization. A range Of contextual strategies is employed at the national and 
at State levels for generating awareness and promoting behaviour change. 
In order to strengthen the ongoing communication efforts, a 
Communication Consortium on HIV/AIDS has been set up to bring together a 
number of partners so that sufficient funds could be mobilized. UNICEF acts as 
the secretariat for the consortium. An agreement to this effect has 
4 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 [18 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
been signed between NACO and UNICEF on 9.11.2004. The objectives of the Consortium 
are:— 
(i) Bring knowledge and awareness on HIV/AIDS to all the people of India 
within the shortest possible time through fast and intensified media 
interventions and campaigns. 
(ii) Involve youth in as many creative ways as possible in the prevention 
and management of HIV/AIDS. 
(iii) Organize caravans and road shows (involving trains, buses, tractors and 
bullock carts) to suit specific needs and sensitivities of different unreached 
segments of population especially the adolescents and youth. 
(iv) Bring together alliances and partnerships already working on the subject as 
strategic and area specific and effective coalitions for action. 
SHRIMATI S.G INDIRA: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I thank you very much. On seeing the 
answer of the hon. Minister, I find that the National AIDS Control Programme, Phase-ll gives 
the highest priority to generate awareness about HIV/AIDS. Sir, the first case of HIV was 
detected in 1986. Now this number reached upto 5.1 million at the end of the last year. 
India today has stood next only to South Africa, which is estimated to have 5.4 million cases 
of HIV/AIDS. This shows-that we have failed somewhere to check the growth of 
HIV/AIDS. According to a report released by the World Health Organisation on the 
assessment for the year 2004, it has been revealed that there is insufficient progress in 
expanding retro-viral treatment. What is the Government going to do to expand the retro-
viral treatment for the HIV/AIDS patient in the country? 
DR. ANBUMANI RAMADOSS: Sir, from one case of HIV/AIDS in 1986, today India 
has an estimated case of 5.1 million. Though prevalence-wise it is much lower than many 
other countries in the world, because of the sheer population of the country the numbers 
are quite high. Today, India stands second in the world number-wise but prevalence-wise it 
is just 0.9 per cent of the adult population and 0.5 per cent of the total population. 
Whereas in different countries like Africa it is 23 per cent and in some countries it is 
32 per cent also. The Government is taking all steps to prevent spread and rise of 
HIV/AIDS and we had the first national programme 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [18 March, 2005] 
started in 1992 and the second programme in 1999. In the second programme, we had 
a budgetary allocation of Rs. 2064 crores which ended last year and we are going to the third 
programme next year. All our focuses are on prevention. I reiterate that the Government of India 
is going to spend 85 per cent of its resources and energy on prevention and 15 per cent on 
care and support which is treatment. Hon. Member says that there have not been free ARTs 
given. The Government has committed that they will treat 100,000 people free of cost in 
the next five years and we are going according to the schedule. Till today, about 25 hospitals 
around the country are giving free ARTs, mostly in the high incidence States and by the end of 
this year about 100 hospitals will be giving free ARTs. There is no dearth on that. 
 
SHRIMATI S.G INDIRA: Sir, my second supplementary is that there was an article 
reported in The Hindu on 17.3.2005 by Dr. Sunithis Solomon.  She has mentioned that two 
drugs have been given to a pregnant lady who  is affected by HIV/AIDS four weeks before 
delivery and Neverapin a few  hours before delivery. My question is: economically well 
off people can  consume those medicines on their own but what about the poor ladies  
who have been affected by the HIV/AIDS? Is the Government coming  forward to 
provide all these medicines to Government hospitals all over the  country?  
DR. ANBUMANI RAMADOSS: Sir, the scheme of parent to child transmission 
whereby free Neverapin is given was started way back in 2001 itself, even before the free 
ARTs were given for all the other population. In fact, till today 2888 centres around the country 
are providing free retroviral treatment for pregnant mothers. During delivery Neverapin is 
given just before delivery and after 72 hours the baby is given, whereby a lot of percentage 
of babies getting infected by HIV is reduced. So 288 hospitals around the country are already 
providing for the last four to five years. We are giving it free. 
DR. KARAN SINGH: Sir, to meetthe.growing menace of AIDS, which is creating havoc

widely accepted around the world that the only effective way to prevent the spread of 
AIDS is to have a widespread condom promotion programme. That is what they did

in Thailand. For some strange reason the Ministry seems to be either shy or reluctant to use 
the word 'condom*. In all these replies which they give, they never mention anything about

DR. ANBUMANI RAMADOSS: Sir, the Government is not shy of condoms. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Who is shy? 
DR. ANBUMANI RAMADOSS: The reply is question-specific. The 
Government is promoting 100 per cent condom usage in the country. Unlike the 
previous NDA Government's policy, the UPA Government is going in for 100 per cent

THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) to 
(d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) The National Commission on Farmers headed by Dr. M.S. 
Swaminathan has submitted its first interim report which covers a number of 
issues concerning farmers and their livelihood. The Government of India has 
already taken a number of steps to address the four priority issues 
highlighted. Rural indebtedness, which is one of the primary factors behind 
the distress of farmers has been addressed by raising the volume of rural 
credit by 30 percent during 2004-05. Rescheduling of loans, one time 
settlement have been the other interventions in this regard. The National 
Agriculture insurance Scheme is being strengthened and made multi-pronged 
so as to provide an optimized safety net to farmers. Dryland farming has been 
identified as a key intervention in the Annual Plan of the Department of 
Agriculture for which 200 crores is being provided. For micro-irrigation, 
which will further optimize the benefits  of dryland farming, another 400 
crores has been provided. Rs. 630 crores is being provided for the National 
Horticulture Mission which will raise incomes, provide employment and help 
improve nutritional status in the rural areas which cumulatively will help 
ameliorate distress and promote welfare of farmers. 
The issues concerning creation of legal rights for women in land and 
mainstreaming gender concern in agriculture is receiving Government's 
attention. The Union Budget has already mentioned measures to be taken for 
strengthening the ICDS programme and further enhancement of the nutritional 
and food security network are among Government's top most priority efforts. 
The Ministry of Agriculture has taken on board the involvement of 
Panchayati Raj institutions in its initiati ves to the extent possible. There is a 
provision for involvement of panchayat members in Watershed Committees. 
In many of the ATMA (Agricultural Technology Management Agency) districts, 
members of panchayats are involved in field extension activities.

small and marginal, triggering agricultural growth led economic progress, 
which can lead to opportunities for a healthy and productive life to rural

semi-arid regions, as well as for farmers in hilly and coastal areas in order to link

Technology Missions like those relating to pulses, oilseeds, maize, cotton, 
watershed etc. and recommend methods of promoting horizontal integration of 
vertically structured programmes. Also, suggest credit-linked insurance 
schemes, which can protect resource poor farm families from unbearable 
risks. Further, suggest methods of strengthening and streamling the National

The Commission has submitted its first interim report. The Government of 
India has already taken a number of steps to address priority issues highlighted 
in the report. Rural indebtedness, which is one of the primary factors behind the 
distress of farmers has been addressed by raising the volume of rural credit by 
30 per cent during 2004-05. Rescheduling of loans, one time settlement have 
been the other interventions in this regard. The National Agriculture Insurance 
Scheme is being strengthened and made multi-pronged so as to provide an 
optimized safety net to farmers. Dryland farming has been identified as a key 
intervention in the Annual Plan of the Department of Agriculture for which 200 
crores is being provided. For micro-irrigation, which will further optimize the benefits 
of dryland farming another 400 crores has been provided. Rs. 630 crores is being 
provided for the National Horticulture  Mission which will raise incomes, 
provide employment and help improve nutritional status in the rural areas which 
cumulatively will help ameliorate distress and promote welfare of farmers. 
The issues concerning creation of legal rights for women in land and 
mainstreaming gender concern in agriculture is receiving Government's 
attention. The Union Budget has already mentioned measures to be taken for 
strengthening the ICDS programme and further enhancement of the nutritional 
and food security network are among Government's top most priority efforts. 
The Ministry of Agriculture has taken on board the involvement of 
Panchayati Raj institutions in its initiatives to the extent possible. There is a 
provision for involvement of panchayat members in Watershed Committees. 
In many of the ATMA (Agricultural Technology Management Agency) districts, 
members of panchayats are involved in field extension activities.

Model Act on agricultural marketing 
*245.  SHRIMATI JAMANA DEVI BARUPAL 
† DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE  be pleased to state: 
(a) whether in January, Government have circulated a Model Act on 
agricultural marketing asking States to amend their laws and allow private players 
to set markets for sale of farm produce; 
(b) whether launching of Horticulture Mission and a new Weather 
Insurance Scheme would be more beneficial for Indian agriculture; and 
(c) if so, the other steps being considered by Government to improve 
agricultural sector in year 2005-06? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) to 
(c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. Under the existing Agricultural Produce Market (Regulation) Act 
(APMC Act), State Government alone is empowered to initiate the process of setting 
up of markets for agricultural commodities in notified areas. Processing 
industry can not buy directly from the farmers. The farmer is restricted from 
entering into direct contract with any manufacturer as the produce is required to 
be canalized through regulated markets. These restrictions are acting as a 
disincentive to farmers, trade and industries. The Governments have, therefore, 
been advised to amend the APMC Act to allow direct marketing and contract 
farming and to permit setting up of competitive markets in private and 
cooperative sectors. A Model APMC Act has also been circulated by this 
Ministry to all the States to guide them in implementation of the suggested 
reforms. The Model Act enable any person, grower and local authority to establish 
new market in any area, removes compulsion on growers to sell their produce 
through existing regulated markets, allows establishment of direct purchase 
centres and farmers of markets for direct sale, promote public private 
partnership in management and development of markets, establish special 
markets for commodities like onion, fruits, vegetables, flowers etc. This matter 
was

Devi Barupal.

discussed at the national conference of State Ministers on 19.11.2004. All the 
States have in general agreed for bringing about proposed reforms in the 
Agricultural Marketing sector. 
(b) Yes Sir, The National Horticulture Mission is expected to be launched 
in April, 2005. The basic objective of the National Horticutlure Mission 
(NHM) is to double the horticulture production by 2011-12. The Mission 
envisages technological interventions through forward and back linkages 
duly addressing all the links from production to marketing and processing 
of horticultural produce, with an es timated production of 300 million tones 
by 2011 -12. The Mission would specially address (a) Horticultural Research, 
(b) Horticultural development through generation of good quality seeds 
and planting material, coverage of area with improved varieties, productivity 
improvement programmes, human resource development and 
demonstration (c) Post Harvest Management and Marketing by creating 
infrastructure facilities for cool chai n, market yards & market intelligence 
and (d) Value addition & Processing of horticulture produce to reduce 
losses and add value to the product. 
The basic idea of Weather Insurance is to estimate the percentage deviation 
in crop output due to adverse deviation in weather conditons. Techniques like 
multivariate regression could explain the impact of weather deviations/variations 
on productivity. This gives the linkage between the financial losses suffered by 
farmers due to weather variations and also estimates the indemnities that will 
be payable to them. The Joint Group constituted to study the improvements 
required in the existing crop insuran ce scheme has considered the Weather 
Insurance and found it suitable in speci fic areas/crops. The Government is 
consulting various stakeholders regarding implementation of the 
recommendations of the Group. 
(c) Department has proposed to carry forward new interventions/new 
schemes alongwith ongoing programmes in the Annual Plan 2005-06, for 
which the Plan outlay has been enhanced considerably to Rs 4179.32 
crore as against the RE outlay of Rs 2945.00 crore in 2004-05. The new 
package for the agriculture sector includes the National Horticulture 
Mission, Micro-irrigation, National Mission on Bamboo, Enhancing 
sustainability of Dry land/Rainfed Farming System and increased flow of 
Rural Credit. Initiatives under the Indian Council of Agricltural Research

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI 
RAMDOSS): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
The Government of India-WHO Collaborative Programme has carried out a 
multicentric study in 10 sites in India, including Delhi, to identify the health 
problems of the elderly.The objectives of the study were:— 
(a) to assess the morbidity profile of geriatric population (60 years and 
above); 
(b) to study the current level of health care facilities available and the 
perceived needs of the elderly; and 
(c) to suggest means for geriatric health services suitable for rural/ urban 
community. 
The Delhi site study was carried out by Maulana Azad Medical College. The 
study has brought out major health problems seen in the elderly Indians. The 
Common co-morbid diseases associated  with elderly population showed a 
prevalence of Ischemic Heart Disease (30%), Diabetes (19%), Hypertension 
(15.6%), COPD/Asthma (21%) and T.B. (6.4%). The study has also revealed a 
high prevalence of knee osteoarthiritis and CNS problems such as dizziness. The 
outcomes of the study has brought out the need for making geriatrics a 
superspeciality, in view of the multiplicity of problems requiring special care and 
attention. Since these diseases are related to life style practices, the Government is 
creating health awareness amongst the people through the media, including 
electronic media. Government is also in the process of formulating a National 
Programme for Diabetes and Cardio Vascular Diseases in which the needs of 
older citizens will also be addressed.

Statement-I 
Report of the World-wide Funds for Nature-India regarding tiger population in 
Sariska 
In response to an invitation from the PCCF Rajasthan, a team from 
WWF—India visited Sariska tiger Reserve on 11th and 12th February to assist 
in the intensive search operations undertaken by Government from 1—15 
February 2005 of locating tigers in the Sariska Tiger Reserve. The WWF—India 
team searched the entire area of the erstwhile stronghold of the tiger from 
Kamavas-Kalighati-Salopka-Pandupoleon both sides of the road and made the 
following observations: 
1. It had been earlier claimed that about 300 persons had been 
employed in the search operations. The team saw no evidence of any 
intensive efforts being made by the Park authorities on 11th and 
12th February 2005. 
2. The area searched by the team: both during day and night time, revealed 
not a single sign of evidence, direct or indirect to indicate the continued 
presence of tiger in the areas that were the tiger's stronghold up to the 
first half of 2004. Discussions revealed that the search operations 
carried out by the staff had also drawn similar conclusions. 
3. The last two reported sightings of tigers were on 14 July 2004 at the 
Salopka anicut and on 26 August 2004 near kalighati Chowki. 
39 

RAJYA SABHA [18 March, 2005] 
4. The entire area where once tigers roamed had cattle grazing freely. Head leads 
of wood were being removed by villagers even from areas where the personnel 
of the forest department are present on a permanent basis. This activity was 
seen within 500 meters of the entry gate on a day when even the Chief Wildlife 
warden was present in Sariska. 
5. The forest staff were extremely reluctant to give any explanation for the 
disappearance of the tiger but tended to agree on the following 
possibilities: 
 
• The damage to the Park's tigers has taken place between July 2004 and 
December 2004. 
• The presence of 18 tigers as claimed by the Park in 2004 was 
probably an over estimation. 
• Poaching during the defined period can be the principal cause for the 
sudden disappearance of the tiger. 
• Negligence by the forest staff in regular monitoring is likely. Connivance 
of the lower staff with the poachers cannot be ruled out. 
6. There appears to be a systemic failure in the Park's management. 
. Also the morale of the grassroots staff is at its lowest ebb. 
7. 11-13 samples of scats had been collected by the forest staff during their 
search to WWF- India operation. All these were seen by the team. Only two of 
these appeared to be of tiges. However, as the shape had been disturbed during 
collection and later handling, a visual confirmation was not considered prudent 
and laboratory analysis by Wll is recommended. It would necessary to mention 
that both the samples in question were fairly old. 
8. The forest guard at Salopka *Chowki described scratch mark he had seen on 
top of the adjoining hill. The length of the mark indicated that it may have 
been made by a tiger. 
9. We were informed that a villager by the name of Sriram had seen a tigress 
in the area known as Aalgwal. When contacted by the team, the person 
confirmed that he did see a large cat a few days back but was not in a 
position to confirm whether it was a tiger or a leopard. 
40 

[18 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
10. The staff also confirmed that the leopard was being seen more freely 
in areas that were once the excl usive domain of the tiger. This 
indicates the absence of the tiger from these areas. 
11. The postings of senior Park staff carried out on orders of the State 
Government need to be considered as one of the contributory 
causes. 
 
• Shri Raghubir Singh Sekhawat served as the Deputy Director for a brief 
period from end February to May 2004. On being posted out in May 
04, the post remained vacant till September 04. This is the crucial 
period during which most of the damage is believed to have taken 
place. 
• In September, 04 the present Field Director, Shri S.K. Jain and the 
Deputy Director, Shri Priya Ranjan were posted in together. Both were 
new to the Park as they had not served in the area earlier. This 
caused some difficulty in management at the Park Headquarters 
level. 
• A decision has now been taken to shift the Park Headquarters to 
Jaipur and that of the Deputy Director to Alwar. This will be 
counterproductive. 
Conclusion and recommendations 
1. The damage to Sariska Tiger Reserve is likely to have taken place 
between July and December 2004. If any tigers remain, their 
numbers are likely to be small. 
2. There appears to be a systemic failure of the Park's management. Grazing 
and woodcutting is rampant and is taking place right in front of the 
staff who lack motivation and have an extremely low morale. 
3. The need to adopt all possible measures to counter poaching cannot 
be over emphasized. While looking outwards for possible poachers, it 
may also be prudent to look inwards for possible involvement of 
the staff. 
4. The decision to relocate the field Director and the Deputy Director needs 
reconsideration. 
41 

RAJYA SABHA [18 March, 2005] 
5. The Park still has no priority for the management of Cores 2 & 3. This 
needs to be corrected. 
6. The relocation of villages pending since many years needs to be 
executed forthwith. 
7. The top management must stay at Sariska and take up the 
challenge of rebuilding the Park. 
8. Establish a core management Committee comprising of naturalists 
and conservation supporters who should hold quarterly meetings. Reports 
and feedback from the forest department and senior Govt, officials. 
9. Make committee findigns public/involve people from Rajasthan who 
should play a constructive role. 
 
10. Greater emphasis must be laid on patrolling and field leadership. 
11. A fresh Management Plan for Sariska be made with inputs from the 
Committee. 
12. Improve the corridor between Sariska and Ranthambore. 
13. Activate the State Wildlife Advisory Board. 
14. In case conditions do not improve by May 2005, a fresh plan of action 
be considered.

the practice of pre-birth elimination of females. Acomprehensive Act known as Pre-

for the prohibition of sex selection, before or after 
43

conception, and for regulation of pre-natal diagnostic techniques for the purpose 
of detecting certain abnormalities and for the prevention of their misuse for sex

the Appropriate Authorities appointed under the Act at State, District as well as 
Sub-district levels. The violators of the Act are punishable with imprisonment 
upto 5 years and fine upto Rs. 5 lakhs, alongwith cancellation of registration of

country. There are 300'ongoing Court/Police Cases and 33 machines

organized at State/regional/district/block levels to create awareness against this 
social evil. Cooperation has also been sought from religious leaders, as well as 
medical fraternity to curb this practice. The Government of India has

pirces. The Drugs (Prices Control) Orders have been issued in accordance with

The 74 bulk drugs specified in the First Schedule of the Drugs (Prices

†1865. SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state:

country during the last nine years; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and

agricultural growth rate? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) The agricultural growth rate in the country has 
not shown any consistent trend during the last nine years. The details of growth 
rate of GDP in agriculture including allied sectors are given in the Statement. (See 
below) 
(b) Since about 60% of the net so wn area is rain-fed, agricultural 
production is heavily influenced by rainfall. During the last nine years, the 
growth rate in agriculture was negative in four years, namely, 1995-96 (-
0.9)%, 1997-98 (-2.4%), 2000-01 (-0.1%) and 2002-03 (-7.0%). The main reason 
for the negative growth rate in 1995-96 was the significant decline in the 
production of both kharif and rabi foodgrains, whereas in 1997-98 and in 2000-
01 the main reasons was the significant decline in the production of rabi foodgrains 
and oilseeds. The year 2002-03 witnessed a severe

drought that affected several States in the country, and was responsible for the 
sharp decline in agricultural productio n. The low percentage of area under 
irrigation in respect of major crops, particularly oilseeds (23.0 per cent) and 
pulses (about 13 per cent) in the country as a whole and the wide inter-
State/regional differentials in irrigated area have contributed to the negative 
agricultural growth in the years referred to above. 
(c) With a view to increasing agricultural production, the Government have 
identified thrust areas for focused and priority attention, which include agricultural credit, 
irrigation, horticulture, and marketing reforms. The Union Budget for 2005-06 has

banks, regional rural banks and cooperative banks towards providing credit, 
especially production credit, to farm households. The other areas highlighted in the 
Budget include micro irrigation technology comprising drip and sprinkler irrigation, 
National horticulture Mission with focus backward and forward linkages, and 
development/strengthening of agricultural marketing infrastructure, grading and 
standardization.

National Fertilizer Policy 
1868. SHRI SUDARSHAN AKARAPU: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have formulated/finalized the new National 
Fertilizer Policy; 
(b) if so, the salient features thereof; and 
(c) if not, the time-frame by which the policy would come into effect? 
 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALSAND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM VILAS 
PASWAN): (a) to (c) Payment of subsidy to indigenous manufacturers of urea is 
regulated under the provisions of the New Pricing Scheme (NPS) for urea units. 
Concession to manufacturers and importers of decontrolled phosphatic and 
potassic fertilizers is made under the provisions of the Scheme of Concession 
on sale of decontrolled phosphatic and potassic fertilizers. NPS was introduced 
w.e.f. 1.4.2003 replacing the erstwhile Retention Price Scheme. NPS is being 
implemented in stages. Stage-I was of one year duration, from 1.4.2003 to 
31.3.2004. Stage-ll is of two years duration, from 1.4.2004 to 31.3.2006. 
 
A Working Group has been constituted on 10.12.2004 under the 
chairmanship of Dr. Y.K. Alagh to review the effectiveness of Stage-I and II of 
New Pricing Scheme (NPS) for urea units and to formulate a policy for urea units 
for Stage-Ill commencing from 1.4.2006. The Working Group would also 
examine issues pertaining to formulation of feedstock policy especially with 
regard to nature, pricing and availability, demand and supply of urea upto the end of 
11 th Five Year Plan, fixing milestones for conversion of existing naphtha and 
FO/LSHS based units to NG/LNG, mode of determination and methodology of 
payment of concession to urea units, de-control of movement and distribution 
of urea; balanced fertilization through urea pricing etc. The Working Group has 
been asked to submit its report within six months from the date of its 
constitution. 
 
A policy has been announced for setting up new urea projects and 
expansion of existing urea projects for augmenting the domestic production 
62 

[18 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
capacity of urea to meet the growing demand for enhancing the agricultural 
production in the country. The new and expansion urea units will be based on 
natural.gas/LNG as feedstock which is the most cost effective and the least 
polluting feedstock in fertilizer sector today. The new policy will enable the 
entrepreneurs to decide about their investment plans in the fertilizer sector. 
Policy has also been announced for de-bottlenecking/revamp/ 
modernization of existing urea units, which will be allowed only if the 
additional production comes from using natural gas/LNG as feedstock. 
Government has also formulated a policy for conversion of existing 
naphtha/FO/LSHS based urea units to natural gas/LNG as feedstock. The 
plants based on naphtha/FO/LSHS are less energy efficient and have a higher 
production cost. Therefore, the policy encourages an early conversion to 
natural gas/LNG so that they acquire a competitive edge in the deregulated and 
liberalised economic scenario. With a view to encouraging investments for 
switchover to NG/LNG as feedstock, the investor is assured that savings on 
account of energy efficiency after conversion would be retained by the plants 
for a maximum period of 5 years in respect of naphtha based plants and 10 
years in respect of FO/ LSHS based plants.

1874. SHRIN. R. GOVINDRAJAR: W ill the Minister of CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the production cost of chemicals and fertilizers in the 
country is higher than the international level; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) whether Government had made efforts to find out the cost of 
production of chemicals and fertilizers in the developed countries? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM VILAS 
PASWAN): (a) to (c) Chemical industry has been delicensed except three 
hazardous chemicals. There is no control of the Government on production 
74 

[18 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
and pricing of chemicals. Therefore, cost of production of chemicals is not 
monitored by the Government. 
As far as the production cost of fertilizers in the country is concerned, it is 
dependent on the type of feedstock used and its cost. Costlier the feedstock, 
more is the cost of production of indigenous fertilizers. At present, the cost of 
production of indigenous urea is less than the cost of imported urea. The present 
weighted average cost of production of indigenous urea is Rs. 8494 per metric 
tonne, the cost (C & F) of imported urea is Rs. 11073 per metric tonne. There 
is no separate monitoring of cost of production of fertilizers in other 
countries. 
The country is totally dependent on imports for manufacturing its 
indigenous Di-Ammonium Phosphate (DAP). Almost entire quantity of 
ammonia and phosphoric acid is imported by DAP manfuacturers. Similarly, 
the units, which use rock phosphate and manufacture their own phosphoric acid, 
are also dependent upon imported rock phosphate and imported sulphur for their 
entire requirement. Thus, the cost of indigenous DAP is primarily dependent upon 
the prices of raw material/intermediates prevailing in the international market.

Factories affecting the quality of water in metro cities 
1895.  SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: 
SHRI RAJU PARMAR: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government are fully aware of the fact that a large number of 
factories have affected the quality of water in the metropolitan cities; 
(b) whether it is fact that water in many metropolitan and capital cities has 
been unpotable due to affluents discharged by these factories; and 
(c) if so, the steps Government have taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) to (c) The industries 
discharging waste water have been identfied by the State Pollution Control 
Boards/Pollution Control Committee. These industries have been directed by the 
concerned State Pollution Control Board/Pollution Control Committee to set-
up requisite pollution control measures. The effluent discharge standards 
have been stipulated for these industries and concerned State Pollution 
Control Boards/Pollution Control Committees have directed these units to set up 
requisite pollution control equipments. In case of non-co mpliance necessary 
legal actions are initiated as per Drovisions of various environmental Acts. 
99 

RAJYA SABHA [18 March, 2005] 
Accumulation of e-wastes 
1896. SHRI S.RM. SYED KHAN: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the accumulating electronic wastes which 
are hazardous to health; 
(b) whether Government have developed any system to deal e-wastes; and 
(c) the steps taken by Government to tackle the e-wastes threat? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) As electronic wastes 
contain substances such as Lead, Cadmium, Mercury, Poly Chlorinated 
Biphenyls (PCB).-Pol Vinyl Chloride (PVC) etc., they have the potential to cause 
harm to human health and environment if not handled properly. 
(b) and (c) As the collection and recycling of electronic wastes is being done 
by the informal sector in our country at present, the Government has taken the 
following steps to deal with and tackee the e-wastes threat:— 
• Electronic wastes are included under List A and List B of 
Schedule-3 of the Hazardous Wastes (Management and Handling) 
Rules, 1989 as amended from time to time. The import of this waste is 
therefore regulated by the Ministry of Environment and Forests and no 
permission has been granted by the Ministry till date for such imports 
• Subsequent to the organization of a National Workshop on 
Electronic Waste Management, action has been initiated by the Central 
Pollution Control Board (CPCB) for rapid assessment of the e-waste 
generated in major cities of the country. 
• A National Working Group consisting of regulatory agencies, 
NGOs, Industry Associations, experts and recyclers has also been 
constituted by CPCB for formulating a strategy and road map for 
management of electric and electronic wastes in an 
environmentally sound manner. 
• A comprehensive technical guide on "Environmental Management for 
Information Technology Industry in India" has been published 
100 

[18 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
and circulated widely by the Department of Information 
Technology (DIT), Ministry of Communication and Information 
Technology. 
• A demonstration project has also been set up by the DIT at the Indian 
Telephone Industries, Palakkad, Kerala for recovery of copper from 
Printed Circuit Boards. 
• Several workshops and seminars have been organized in different 
parts of the country by the DIT on Environmental Management in 
Electronics Industry. 
Report on drying water lands 
1897. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that according to the Report, Inland Water Lands of 
India-Conservation Priorities by SalimAli Centre for Ornithology and Natural 
History, the water lands have been drying in 14 States of the country; 
(b) if so, the details of the report; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that the Report recommended for having a 
national policy on this; 
(d) if so, the details thereon; and 
(e) the details of wet lands in the the country as on 1st January, 1980 and as 
on 1st January, 2005? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) and (b) The Report entitled 
"Inland Water Lands of India-Conservation Priorities" by Salim Ali Centre for 
Ornithology and Natural History (SACON) presents information about wetlands 
of the size of 2 hectares and above in 72 districts located in 10 States. Wetlands 
in 33 districts in the studied category are reported to have undergone spatial 
reduction. However, there is no corroborative evidence of these findings. 
(c) and (d) The SACON's report recommends formulation of National Policy 
on Wetlands. Some of the suggestions made thereon relate to 
101 

RAJYA SABHA [18 March, 2005] 
creation of National Wetland Authority, National Wetlands Biodiversity 
Register, prioritization of wetlands a nd capacity building in management 
planning of wetlands. 
(e) The details of wetlands with reference to time-frames of 1 st January, 1980 
and 1st January, 2005 are not available in the absence of any specific study in this 
regard. 
Guidelines allowing developmental/construction activities in 
forests 
1898. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to refer to answer to Unstarred 
Question 517 given in the Rajya Sabha on the 4th March, 2005 and state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Ministry has also allowed to cut trees in the 
forest areas; 
(b) whether any consultations with the State Governments have been held in 
this respect; and 
(c) if so, the outcome of such consultations? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMONARAINMEENA): (a) to (c) On the persistent 
requests of the various State/UT Governments, and various Central 
Government Ministries, the Ministry of Environment and Forests vide letter dated 
03.01.2005, considered general appr oval under Section 2 of the Forest 
(Conservation) Act, 1980, and permitted the State/UT Governments to proceed 
with need based diversion of forest land below one hectare in each case, in 
favour of Government Departments for construction of public welfare 
amenities like schools, dispensary/hospital, electric and telecommunication lines, 
drinking water projects, water/rainwater harvesting structures, minor irrigation 
canal, non-conventional sources of energy, skill upgradation/vocational training 
centre, power sub-stations, communication posts, and police establishments like 
police stations/outposts/border outposts/watch towers, in sensitive areas 
(identified by Ministry of Home Affairs). While granting general approval, the 
Central Government also considered the fact that such construction of public 
welfare projects may also involve felling of trees. 
102 

[18 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
To check indiscriminate felling of trees, the Central Government has also 
prescribed the upper ceiling on number of trees that can be felled to facilitate 
execution of the public welfare work. Maximum number of trees that can be 
removed in respected of each project should not exceed fifty per hectare.lt has also 
been stipulated that corresponding permissible limit of maximum number of trees 
to be felled for the forest area diverted, shall be in proportion to the extent of 
the diverted area. Further, to mitigate the ill-effects of such felling, it has also 
been made mandatory for the user agency to plant and maintain two times the 
number of trees felled on the diverted land at the project co st in consultation 
with the State Forest Department.

Threat of prowling animals in Pir Panjal range 
1904.  SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: 
SHRI AMAR SINGH: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that residents of border areas on the hills of 
Pir Panjal range bordering Rajouri, Doda and Poonch districts in Jammu and 
Kashmir are constantly living under the threat of prowling wild animals with out 
little help from wild life department; 
111 

RAJYA SABHA [18 March, 2005] 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor and how many persons have actually 
been killed/injured by wild animals during the last three years; and 
(c) the remedial steps Government propose to take to ensure the safety 
of villagers in those areas? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) and (b) Due to 
unprecedented snow fall this year on the mountain ranges of Pir Panjal Range, 
several animals migrated to lower altitudes. As a result, there has been a marginal 
increase in the attack on human beings by these animals. As reported by State 
Government in last three years, 19 cases of human killing have been reported 
due to attack by wild animals. 
(c) Following steps have been taken by the Government to ensure safety of 
villagers in the affected areas- 
• Increased awareness among the villagers about the behaviour of the wild 
animals. 
• Mobile anti-poaching and rescue squads have been provided.

Recommendations of Swaminathan Committee 
1907. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: 
SHRI B. J. PANDA: 
SHRIDATTAMEGHE: 
DR. MAM. RAMASWAMY: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that recently the M.S. Swaminathan Committee on coastal 
regulation system has suggested inter-alia 'bio-shields' like mangroves to protect 
India's coastal areas and cautioned against unregulated development activities to 
prevent disasters like Tsunami; 
(b) whether the Committee has submitted its report; 
118 

[18 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) if so, the details of other major recommendations made by the 
Committee; and 
(d) the action taken/proposed to be taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) The main recommendations of the Committee inter-alia include: 
(i) Ecological and cultural security, livelihood security and national 
security should be the cornerstones of the Integrated Coastal Zone 
Management Policy. 
(ii) The coastal zone should include the water area upto the teimtorial limits 
on the seaward side and upto the administrative boundaries or biological 
boundaries on the landward side of the sea coast. The coastal zone 
management should include the inland water bodies and the land area 
along such water bodies. 
(iii) Regulation, education and social mobilization should be the three major 
components of a participatory and sustainable coastal zone 
management strategy. 
(iv) Protection and sustainable development in marine and coastal 
environment and its resources should be in conformity with 
international law. 
(v) The coastal regulation needs to be based on sound scientific and 
ecological principles and should safeguard both natural and cultural 
heritage. 
(vi) Precautionary approach should be used where there are potential threats 
of serious irreversible damage. 
(vii) Significant or irreversible risk and harm to human health and life 
critical systems and resources including cultural and heritage would 
be considered unacceptable. 
(viii) Coastal policy and regulations should be guided by the principles of 
gender and social equity. 
(ix) Coastal protection and bio-resources conservation should be guided by 
techno-econmic efficiency, precautionary approach, "polluter pays" 
and "public trust" doctrine. 
119 

RAJYA SABHA [18 March, 2005] 
(x) Principles contained in the Biodiversity Act, 2002 should be 
applied to coastal bio-resources management. 
(xi) Regeneration of mangrove wetlands, coral reefs, seagrass beds as well 
as coastal forestry and agro forestry will confer both short and long 
term ecological and livelihood benefits. 
(xii) In view of the severe loss of life and livelihood due to Tsunami, short 
term commercial interest should not be allowed to undermine the 
ecological security of our coastal areas. 
(d) An in-depth examination of the recommendations contained in the 
Report would be required before taking any action.

1923. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that more than 60 per cent of injections 
administered in various hospitals are unsafe according to a World Bank funded 
study; 
(b) if so, the complete details thereof; 
(c) whether the study of Indian National Injections Safety Association has 
also found that safety of injections in India is poorest at immunization clinics; 
and 
(d) if so, the steps Government have taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. As per 
findings of the study, funded by the World Bank and conducted by INCLEN, 69 per 
cent of injections given at Government Hospitals are unsafe. Half of this is due to 
(i) use of un-sterilized syringes and reuse of syringes and other half due to (ii) 
wrong injection practices namely (a) flushing syringes needle before use (b) 
wiping the needle (c) touching the needle surface (d) syringe and needle used on 
more than one patient (e) picking of glass syringe and needle from boiler by hand 
(f) multi dose vial not wiped clean before drawing (g) injections site not cleaned 
(h) recapping needle and (i) not flushing glass syringe after use before re-
sterilization. 
The other findings of the study indicates that immunization accounts for 
17.5 per cent of total injections and 74 per cent of this are unsafe because of 
predominantly use of glass syringes.

No study by Indian National Injection Safety Association has come to the notice of 
the Government of India.

of glass syringes and needles in all immunization clinics in the country in 2005. AD syringes 
will take care of most of the causes of unsafe injections including some due to wrong habits 
as AD syringes are pre-sterilized and cannot be re-used.

Statement-Ill 
Details of various programmes implemented by Ministry for control of 
Cancer, AIDS and T.B. 
National Cancer Control Programme 
In order to control this problem, National Cancer Control Programme was 
launched in 1975 with the objectives of prevention, early detection and 
treatment of cancer in the country. The strategies under the programme are 
awareness generation in the community for prevention and early detection of 
cancer, and provision of comprehensive ca ncer treatment facilities across the 
country by way of supporting Regional Cancer Centres. Government Medical 
Colleges and Government Hospitals are also  supported by Development of 
Oncology Wings. 
167 

RAJYA SABHA [18 March, 2005] 
National AIDS Control Programme 
In order to prevent and control the spread of HIV/AIDS in India, the Goverment of 
India has launched a comprehensive National AIDS Control Programme, currently under 
implementation throughout the country as a centrally sponsored scheme with following 
components:— 
* Preventive interventions for high-risk populations through targeted inverventions 
adopting a multi-pronged stategy including peer counseling and behaviour 
change communication 
* Preventive interventions for the general population through programmes 
for blood safety, voluntary counseling and testing services, Prevention of Parent 
to Child Transmission (PPTCT), Information Education and Communication 
(IEC) & awareness building among adolescents and sensitization for the 
AIDS Vaccine Initiative. 
* Provision of low cost care and support services by providing community 
care services, treatment of opportunistic infections and prevention of 
occupational exposure. 
* Collaborative efforts to promote inter-sectoral programme activities 
including workplace interventions and public-private partnerships. 
* Build technical and managerial capacities for programme 
implementation through Surveillance, Training, Monitoring and Evaluation, 
Technical resource groups, operational research and Programme 
management. 
National TB Control Programme 
To control TB, National Tuberculosis Control Programme (NTCP) was launched in the 
country in 1962. This could not achieve the desired results. Therefore, Revised National TB 
Control Programme (RNTCP), widely known as DOTS, which is a WHO recommended 
strategy, with the objective of achieving cure rate of 85% of new sputum positive cases and 
to detect at least 70% of such cases, is being implemented since the year 1997 in a phased 
manner. Diagnosis by sputum microscopy instead of by X-ray helps in detecting and 
curing infectious cases on priority. Facilities for diagnosis by sputum microscopy 
have been decentralized and 
168 

[18 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
strengthened. Drugs are provided under observation and patients are 
monitored so that they complete their treatment. Drugs are provided free of cost 
in patient-wise boxes. Pr esently, more than 950 million population in 547 
districts/reporting units has been covered under the revised strategy. The Project 
districts have reported cure rate of more than 85% which means that more 
than 8 out of every 10 patients put on treatment under the revised strategy are 
being successfully cured as against below 4 in the earlier Programme. To make 
the programme more accessible to larger segments of the population, and to 
supplement the Government efforts in this direction, emphasis is being given to 
also involve medical colleges, all general hospitals, private practitioners and 
NGOs in the programme. It is envisaged to cover the entire country under the 
Revised Strategy during the current year (2005). 
Mashelkar Committee on Spurious Drugs 
1956. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have reviewed the extant laws relating to 
manufacture and sale of spurious and sub-standard drugs, which cause grievous 
hurt or even death; 
(b) if so, the results thereof and the st eps taken/being taken to check the 
menace and make the manufacture and sale of such drugs unprofitable; and 
(c) the details of follow-up steps taken on the recommendation of the R.A. 
Mashelkar Committee which had inter-alia suggested penalties for various 
such offence under the Drugs and Cosmetic Act? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) Under the provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules 
thereunder, it is the responsibility of State Governments through their 
respective Drug Control organizations to regulate manufacture and sale of drugs as 
well as to keep a surveillance over possible movement of spurious/ counterfeit 
drugs. 
Manufacture and sale of spurious /counterfeit drugs is primarily a 
clandestine activity. To this extent, it is difficult to detect the manufacture 
169 

RAJYA SABHA [18 March, 2005] 
or movement of spurious drugs. Any effective action against this activity would 
require continuous surveillance by the regulators and active cooperation from 
the law and order Enforcement machinery in the State. 
Trading in counterfeit product including drugs is reported world over. 
However, keeping in view the serious implications of spurious drugs on public 
health as well as the loss to genuine industry, the Government has taken various 
measures to combat this menace. 
Steps taken by the Government to check the menace of spurious drugs 
(i) The Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, was amended in 1982 to 
incorporate definition of spurious drugs under section 17B besides 
prescribing severe penalties under section 27 of the Act as mentioned 
below:— 
(a) Manufacture and sale of spurio us drugs are punishable for 
imprisonment of a term which shall not be less than five years but 
which may extend to a term of life and with fine which shall not be 
less than Rs. 10,000/- if such drug is likely to cause death or is likely 
to cause such harm as would amount to grievous hurt within the 
meaning of section 320 of I.P.C. 
(b) Any drug deemed to be spurious but not a drug likely to cause death 
of grievous hurt is punishable with an imprisonment for a term which 
shall not be less than three years but which may extend to five years and 
with fine which shall not be less than Rs. 5000/-. 
(ii) Detailed guidelines have been issued to the State Governments to 
undertake focused surveillance over possible movement of spurious drugs. 
(iii) A capacity Building Project through Word Bank Assistance has been 
taken up to provide substantial assistance to State Governments to upgrade drug 
testing facilities or to establish new drug testing laboratories. 
It is expected to increase the number of samples tested in the country from 
about 36,000 samples to 1,00,000 samples per year and to reduce the reporting 
time to less than a month as against the present period from 3 to 6 months. 
(iv) Specific training programme for regulatory officials of State Governments on 
logistics of intelligence work, prosecutions etc. has been conducted 
170 

[18March,2005] . RAJYA SABHA 
with.the assistance of FDA, Maharashtra. This activity is proposed to be 
continued. 
(v) In order to ensure efficient information exchange between drug 
regulatory officers in the country, in respect of licensing, sampling, 
prosecution, etc., a countrywide computer networking project has been 
undertaken by the Central Government. This will enable the Central 
Government to regularly monitor the enforcement activities and recommend 
corrective measures. 
(vi) Pharma industry and trade has been motivated to fight menace of 
spurious drugs as a sh ared responsibility. Number of cases could be 
successfully detected th rough the initiative taken by Pharma industry 
involving hiring of retired intelligence officers. 
(vii) As per the recommendations of Mashelkar Committee, which was 
constituted by the Government in 2003, to examine all aspects relating to the drug 
regulatory system in the country including the problem of spurious/ sub standard 
drugs, a Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha in December, 2003, to amend the 
said Act to provide stricter penalties to the offenders including a maximum 
penalty of capital punishment. It was further recommended to make the 
offences non-bailable and cognizable and to provide for designated courts for 
speedy trial of cases. 
The Cabinet accorded approval for the introduction of Drugs and 
Cosmetics (Amendment) Bill, 2005, in the Parliament subject to certain 
modifications. The Bill is likely to be introduced in the present Budget 
Session of Parliament. 
The proposed amendments will make the law deterrent to the offenders involved 
in the manufacture or sale of spurious drugs. The involvement of enforcing 
agencies like Police will help in speedy investigation to book the culprits and in 
controlling anti-social elements in such activities.

Raw material supply to Steel Companies 
2005. DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY:  
SHRI MOOLCHAND MEENA: 
Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether steel companies, hit by rising cost and supply constraints of 
critical inputs like iron ore and coking coal, may get some support from 
Government;  
(b) if so, whether Government have formulated package for the steel 
manufactures, with a view to make sufficient quatity of raw materials available to 
them at remunerative prices; 
(c) if so, the details thereof and to what extent this has been helpful; and 
(d) whether this package has been incorporated in the revised national steel 
policy? 
THE MINISTER OF STEEL (SHRI RAM VILAS PASWAN): (a) to (c) In a 
deregulated and decontrolled industry, the prices of steel as well as raw materials 
such as iron ore and coking coal are determind by the interplay of market forces. 
Government does not directly intervene to control prices. 
205 

RAJYA SABHA [18 March, 2005] 
12.00 NOON 
Nevertheless, in order to augment the supply of coking coal in the country, 
Government is allocating captive coki ng coal blocks to the iron and steel 
producers. Government has also abolished the custom duty on imports of low 
ash coking coal and the custom duty on high ash coking coal has been reduced 
to 5% in the current budget in a bid to check the rising cost of this item. 
Moreover, there is no shortage of iron ore in the country and Government is 
committed to ensuring adequate availability of iron ore for the steel industry. 
(d) The Revised National Steel Policy (NSP), inter-alia, seeks to remove the 
supply side constraints including iron ore and coking coal for the growth of the 
industry in an open, globally integrated and competitive environment.

SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JOSHI (Maharashtra): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, firstly I must 
express my happiness at the generally high and elevated debate we have had in the House 
on the General Budget. I am also impressed by the fact that so many people have been 
able to understand and grasp what the contents of Budget are and I, like a blind man, trying to 
find out what the elephant is like, is still searching and groping for what the Budget really 
means. For fifty-four years since I became a student of economics, Budget used to be just 
Rs. 200 crores. I have been impressed by the voluminous documentation that is presented and 
the kind of plethora of promises that are made by every Finance Minister. 
As years went by, I have seen that parties come and go, Finance Ministers come 
and go. I have realised that Budgets are, in the modem day, the opium of the masses. 
They send the whole year in an unhappy manner, when the Budget comes, they start 
hoping for something good and they hope every time that something good is coming till 
the next Budget comes; and they realise that their hands are as empty as they were 
one year back. 
The changes that have taken place are about food security—India has become food 
sufficient; longevity has improved; communications have improved. But the poor man 
continues to be, more or less, in the same position as he was fifty years back. Now, I don't 
feel enthused about any of the promises made by the Finance Minister and I was not enthused 
by the whole list of projects that the Finance Minister announced because I found that he was 
really trying to kill three birds with the same kind of stone. Number one, of course, he has 
every right to hit at the NDA and show that his performance is better. But he was trying at the 
same time to please his Leftist friends and at the same time undercut their constituency 
support with a view to the Kerala and West Bengal elections as well. The most important 
question is, if for 50 years the Finance Ministers have failed to deliver on growth, equity 
and stability, what chances has this Budget to give a better performance.

SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JOSHI: I think the most important point is this: 
What are the modalities proposed for bringing the results. The Finance Minister talks 
of the outlays and outputs. I think outlays and outputs are linked with the outlook. 
What is the kind of outlook that you have for bringing about execution of these projects. 
Fifty years back we talked of the paramount importance of the public sector. Then in 1991 
when our present Prime Minister was the Finance Minister, I have a document here 
that was brought out by the Finance Ministry in 1992—where they severely criticised 
the limitations of the public sector and very clearly said that the job of the Government 
is to create an environment that woul d encourage enterprise, initiative and 
efficiency. Now after another 15 years we find in paragraph 8 of the Finance Minister's 
speech—the basic philosophy of this Budget—we reiterate once again the goals of 
stability and equity. But this time the instrument, is the decisive intervention by the 
State. The State is once again the major instrument of policy. What has happened 
since 1991 when the Finance Ministry said that the Government is not an efficient 
way of getting things done? Now we are once again to depend on the Government as a 
prime move of development What has happened and the Finance Minister mentioned 
in his speech was that we have shifted from Jagdish Bhagwat to Amartya Sen. What 
is trying to be done is that instead of saying that the Government is bad in all sectors 
and in all fields, we are trying to find justification for the governmental activity in the 
fields of environment, in the field of employment, in the field of health and in the field 
of education. The question is when do we come to know that this has failed because I 
absolutely have no doubt that anything that depends on the Government machinery, 
the efficiency is bound to fail sooner rather than later. In this connection the concrete 
suggestion I would like to make— which I made to the Planning Commission when 
Eighth Plan was being drafted—is that do not talk of just targets, but also fix 
failure standards. If you are saying that should have one crore hectare of land which 
will be with assured irrigation, also give us a figure that if we do not within five 
years reach even 20 lakh, then we will admit that we have failed and we will take 
disciplinary action against those who were responsible. I think the Budget would 
start making some sense if we provide for failure standards and just tempting people 
with lofty kind of practices that are attached with the Budget Thank you.

continuity. That is why, you will find,  Sir, that programmes started by one 
Government are continued by another Government with, of course, 
modifications. With experience, we try to fine-tune them and improve them. At 
the same time, every Government also undertakes new initiatives. As far as the 
people of India are concerned, they look to the Government; for them Government

In the RE we estimated it as Rs. 52,321 crores. It is broadly about Rs. 52,000 
crores. When it comes to BE 2005-06, Plan plus non-Plan, grants to the States 
are Rs. 78,753 crores. The Government has been obliged to make an additional 
amount of Rs. 26,000 crores as grants to the States. Now, if I was giving loans to 
the States, as under the Eleventh Finance Commission, I would not give these grants 
to the States. The Twelfth Finance Commission has sharply increased the grant 
component and taken away the loan component. Therefore, if you add Rs. 29,003 
crores to the fiscal deficit, you must deduct also the additional grant which I have to 
give. Therefore, the fiscal deficit figure is not understated. The fiscal deficit figure 
correctly reflects the true position. In fact, the Centre takes a hit by this change 
from loan to grant. Why? The Cenre takes a hit becuase Centre's finances as loans 
to States are a capital expenditure which provides assured returns to me; whereas 
grants are revenue expenditure and it provides no returns to me in the 
subsequent years. Therefore, as a result of this changeover from loan to grant, 
the Centre's revenue deficit has, in fact, become high. If we had continued under 
the Eleventh Finance Commission, I would have been able to compress the revenue 
deficit next year. Because we are switching over to the Twelfth Finance Commission, 
I am not able to compress my revenue deficit. That is why, you recall, I said in my 
Budget Speech that I had to press the pause button on the revenue deficit and on 
the fiscal deficit I would be able to compress only 0.2 per cent. But this is 
something which is unavoidable, which will happen in the first year. The bulk of the 
shock is absorbed in the first year. But in the second, third, fouth and fifth years of 
the Twelfth Finance Commission we will be able to come back to the path of fiscal 
correction. I am confident, and I want to assure everyone, particularly, my good friend, 
Dr. Bimal Jalan, and others, that beginning 2006-07 we can resume on the path of 
fiscal correction, both on fiscal deficit and revenue deficit.
